status_summary: The text presumed a continuing USAID with a rebuilt, politically led workforce; instead the agency was wound down, so in the successor structure there is no USAID workforce to which the plan could apply. USAID staff were put on leave from February 2025 (a temporary restraining order extended on 2025-02-13 briefly blocked further leave notices), USAID announced on 2025-03-28 that nearly all positions not required by law would be eliminated through reductions in force effective 2025-07-01 or 2025-09-02, the agency's remaining operations merged into State on 2025-07-01, and GAO reported that USAID staff fell from about 13,600 in January 2025 to 241 in April 2026, with about 730 awards still active in March 2026 and responsibility for them transferred to State. Political leadership did exist (NPR described one appointee serving as USAID Deputy Administrator and State Director of Foreign Assistance who signed the program cancellations), but no USAID Schedule F pilot, SES mobility program, Day One training replacement, Senior Accountable Official or recruiting program was found, so the outcome is the opposite of the text's staffing build-out and the stage is diverged. Litigation continues: a Fourth Circuit stay of 2025-03-28 in the employees' suit against the DOGE dismantling remains in place, and the D.C. Circuit heard argument on 2026-04-23 in AFGE v. Trump (No. 25-5290) with no ruling reported by early October 2026.

timeline.event: A federal judge extended a temporary restraining order, to 2025-02-21, blocking USAID from placing more employees on paid administrative leave, in a suit by AFSA and AFGE; more than 2,000 staff were already locked out of headquarters and systems.

NPR reported that a political appointee serving as USAID Deputy Administrator and State Director of Foreign Assistance signed orders cancelling about 5,200 programs, with directives aiming to shrink the workforce to a couple of hundred people.

Government Executive reported that nearly all USAID positions not required by law would be eliminated through reductions in force effective 2025-07-01 or 2025-09-02, that employees could choose leave from 2025-03-29, and that a circuit court on Friday 2025-03-28 suspended a district court's 2025-03-18 pause on the dismantling (the Fourth Circuit, per Nexstar).
NPR reported that USAID officially shut down and its remaining operations merged into State.

The D.C. Circuit heard argument, mainly on jurisdiction, in the appeal of AFGE v. Trump (No. 25-5290), the challenge to dismantling USAID; AFSA's tracker (updated 2026-10-07) reports no ruling, and says the Fourth Circuit stay of the injunction in J. Doe 4 v. Musk remains with the case in discovery.

GAO reported USAID staffing fell from about 13,600 in January 2025 to 241 in April 2026, and that of 7,510 USAID awards about 730 remained active in March 2026, with responsibility for them transferred to State.

title: Staff USAID with political appointees, a Schedule F pilot and day-one policy training
uncertainties: Searches for a USAID chief human capital officer, Schedule C or Administratively Determined hiring, General Counsel attorney appointments, a Schedule F pilot, SES mobility program, Day One training halt and Senior Accountable Official found nothing specific; the government-wide Schedule Policy/Career program is tracked in c03-01 and the OPM page on it could not be loaded in review. The Fourth Circuit stay date of 2025-03-28 rests on the Government Executive report of that date, which says a circuit court suspended the order on Friday, March 28; the Nexstar copy names the Fourth Circuit but gives only the weekday (a Friday), and the AFSA tracker gives no stay date. The tracker page itself shows an update date of 2026-10-07. GAO does not state how many USAID staff moved to State, and it reports that State could not provide agencywide staffing data; the separation dates of 2025-07-01 and 2025-09-02 come from the March 2025 report, not from later reports of separations carried out. The NPR article names the individual; this record uses office titles only. The 2025 Supreme Court action on foreign aid funds (see c09-02) is separate. Overlap with c09-01 is partial: c09-01 covers the Director of Foreign Assistance structure and the agency's fate, while this record covers the chapter's personnel steps (pp. 271, 278 to 279), which c09-01 does not track.
